claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by near-simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors.
Rapid, synchronized nucleation minimizes the effects of differences in individual-metal reduction kinetics.
Synchronized reduction and nucleation prevent phase separation.
Synchronized reduction and nucleation prevent elemental segregation.
The precursor metals may have different reduction potentials.
A rapid, short-duration activation can cause all metal precursors to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Near-simultaneous reduction produces a transient, uniformly reduced assembly of metal atoms.
The uniformly reduced metal-atom assembly rapidly nucleates into a single-phase alloy.
Metals with disparate reduction kinetics nucleate at different times under unsynchronized processing.
Differential nucleation leads to phase segregation.
Differential nucleation leads to uncontrolled particle morphology.
Differential nucleation leads to high decomposition temperatures.
Rapid synchronized processing should produce uniform high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid synchronized processing should produce a more even elemental distribution than slower processing.
Rapid synchronized processing should produce more regular particle morphology than slower processing.
A slower, unsynchronized baseline should yield phase-separated or elementally segregated structures.
The hypothesis applies when precursor chemistries are compatible enough for kinetically forced simultaneous reduction.
Kinetic forcing can override differences in precursor reduction potentials in applicable systems.
The hypothesis may fail for inherently incompatible elemental chemistries.
Solvent-mediated or other kinetic factors may contribute to alloy formation in addition to rapid reduction.
